A science program on television discussed whether earthquakes can be predicted. A seismologist on the program gave the following hypothetical example:

“The probability that a strong earthquake will occur in the city of Yangiobod in the next thirty years is two out of three.”

(Yangiobod is a made-up city name.)
s0003: Correctly interpreting the meaning of a statement about probability
s0004: A probability does not mean “it will definitely happen” or “when it will happen”. Compare 2/3 with 1/3 (the probability that it does not happen).
s0005: Which of the following best expresses the meaning of the scientist's statement?
s0006: $\frac{2}{3}\cdot 30 = 20$, so there will be an earthquake in Yangiobod in exactly 20 years.
s0007: $\frac{2}{3}$ is greater than $\frac{1}{2}$, so there will definitely be an earthquake in Yangiobod in the next 30 years.
s0008: The probability of an earthquake in Yangiobod in the next 30 years is greater than the probability of no earthquake.
s0009: Nothing can be said, because no one knows exactly when an earthquake will happen.
s0011: The number the scientist gave is a probability, meaning how likely the event is.
s0013: The probability of the opposite event is found by subtracting from one.
s0015: So an earthquake is more likely than no earthquake, but there is no guarantee.
s0016: Answer: C) more likely to happen
s0017: Only answer C interprets the probability correctly.
s0018: Multiplying a probability by a time period makes no sense: a probability does not say in which year the event will happen.
s0019: 2/3 is less than one, so the event is not certain: saying “definitely” is wrong.
s0020: Even if we do not know for sure, a probability lets us judge how likely an event is; this statement rejects the scientist's view.
s0021: An event is certain only if its probability equals 1. Any probability less than 1 only tells “how likely” the event is.
s0023: A small café in Samarkand sells plain vanilla ice cream. If customers wish, they can choose toppings to sprinkle on it. The café has four kinds of toppings: chopped nuts, chocolate chips, raisins and strawberry jam.
s0024: Finding the number of ways to choose two items out of four (combinations)
s0025: Write out all the pairs in an orderly way, and remember that “nuts + raisins” and “raisins + nuts” are the same.
s0026: Dilnoza wants two different toppings on her ice cream. How many different pairs can she choose from?
s0029: First we give the four toppings short labels.
s0031: The nuts form a pair with each of the other three.
s0033: We already counted chocolate with nuts, so we do not repeat it.
s0035: For the raisins, only the strawberry jam is left.
s0038: Dilnoza can choose one of 6 different pairs.
s0039: The answer 12 comes from taking order into account (N–C and C–N are the same pair); 4 or 8 come from not counting all the pairs.
s0040: When order does not matter, the number of pairs is n·(n−1):2.

A school held a qualifying test for the mathematics olympiad. The test is out of 100 points, and a student who scores 50 points or more qualifies. The chart shows the results of classes 9A and 9B (12 students from each class).

The average score of class 9A is 61.5, and that of class 9B is 64.0.

Looking at the chart, the teacher said: “Class 9B did better than class 9A on this test.” The students of 9A disagreed and want to show that 9B did not necessarily do better.
s0043: Finding evidence in a chart from a measure other than the average (number who passed, outlier)
s0044: An average can drop because of a single very low score. Count the bars at 50 and above on the chart.
s0045: Which mathematical argument can the students of 9A make, based on the chart?
s0049: More students qualified in 9A: 11 students, compared with 9 in 9B.
s0050: In 9B, the difference between the highest and lowest scores is smaller than in 9A.
s0051: The average score of 9A is 61.5, which is above 50, so the class did well.
s0052: Class 9A is usually stronger in mathematics, so this result is just chance.
s0053: We add up the 9A bars from 50 upward: 11 students qualified.
s0056: The average of 9A was pulled down by one very low score.
s0058: The fact that more students qualified is a mathematical argument against the teacher's view.
s0059: This difference works in favor of 9B or proves nothing; it is not evidence that 9A did better.
s0060: 61.5 is still less than 64.0; being greater than 50 does not compare the classes.
s0061: This is not a mathematical argument: it is not based on the information in the chart.
s0062: A question like “Who did better?” cannot be answered with one measure (the average); look for other measures in the chart as well.

Javohir is a cycling fan. He looked at the prices at the “Velomarkaz” shop in Tashkent. At the shop you can buy a ready-made bike, or buy four parts separately and assemble the bike yourself: a frame, a wheel set, a chain and gear set, and a brake and handlebar set.

Item — Price (soums)
Ready-made bike — 2 150 000 or 2 400 000
Frame — 900 000, 1 200 000 or 1 350 000
Wheel set (2 wheels) — 380 000 or 720 000
Chain and gear set — 450 000
Brake and handlebar set (brakes, handlebar, cables) — 210 000 or 400 000

(The shop name and prices are hypothetical.)
s0065: Choosing the right values from a table to find the smallest and largest total
s0066: For the cheapest bike, take the cheapest option for each part; for the most expensive, take the most expensive option. The prices of ready-made bikes are not needed here.
s0067: Javohir wants to assemble a bike himself. At this shop, what is the lowest and the highest price of a self-assembled bike, in soums?
s0073: We add the cheapest option for each part.
s0075: There is only one chain and gear set, and we must not forget to add it too.
s0077: Now we take the most expensive option for each part.
s0079: This is how much the most expensive self-assembled bike costs.
s0081: The prices of ready-made bikes have nothing to do with this question.
s0082: These are the prices of ready-made bikes; the question is about a self-assembled bike.
s0083: The chain and gear set (450 000) was not added: even though there is only one option, the bike needs it.
s0084: For the highest price, 1 200 000 was used for the frame instead of 1 350 000.
s0085: In “lowest” and “highest” questions, take the smallest or largest value for each part accordingly, and do not leave out any part.
s0086: Finding the number of different combinations using the multiplication rule
s0087: Write down how many choices there are for each part, and multiply them rather than adding.
s0088: The shop has three kinds of frames, two kinds of wheel sets and two kinds of brake and handlebar sets; there is only one kind of chain and gear set. How many different bikes can Javohir assemble?
s0090: We write down the number of choices for each part.
s0091: For each frame, 2·2 = 4 ways to continue
s0092: Each frame can go with 4 different combinations of wheels and brakes.
s0093: Multiplication rule: the numbers of choices are all multiplied.
s0096: Only the frames and wheels were counted (3·2); the brake and handlebar set was forgotten.
s0097: The choices were added (3+2+2), but they should have been multiplied.
s0098: No correct method leads to 10; perhaps the choices were counted in a disorganized way.
s0099: When several parts are chosen one after another, the numbers of options are multiplied: 3 · 2 · 2.
s0100: Choosing the largest total within a budget
s0101: First check whether the most expensive combination is over budget, then calculate the total for each option and choose the largest one that does not exceed 2 500 000.
s0102: Javohir has 2 500 000 soums. He wants to buy the most expensive self-assembled bike he can afford with this money. Which purchase is correct?
s0103: Frame 1 350 000, wheels 380 000, chain 450 000, brakes and handlebar 210 000
s0104: Frame 1 200 000, wheels 380 000, chain 450 000, brakes and handlebar 400 000
s0105: Frame 900 000, wheels 720 000, chain 450 000, brakes and handlebar 400 000
s0106: Frame 1 350 000, wheels 720 000, chain 450 000, brakes and handlebar 210 000
s0108: The first option fits the budget, but we compare them all.
s0110: The second option also fits and is more expensive.
s0112: The third is more expensive still and does not exceed 2 500 thousand.
s0114: He does not have enough money for the fourth option.
s0116: Of the options that fit, the most expensive is C.
s0117: Taking the most expensive frame seems right, but this purchase totals 2 390 000, which is cheaper than C.
s0118: The total is 2 430 000 soums; it fits the budget, but C (2 470 000) is more expensive.
s0119: The total is 2 730 000 soums, which is 230 000 soums over budget.
s0120: Taking the most expensive part does not always give the most expensive set: compare the totals of all suitable options.
s0122: A staircase going down underground was built at a new metro station in Tashkent. The staircase has 24 identical steps; its total height is 3.84 m and its total length (horizontally) is 7.20 m (see the picture).
s0123: Dividing a total height into equal parts and converting units
s0124: Only the height is needed: the length (7.20 m) is extra information. Convert meters to centimeters and divide by the number of steps.
s0125: What is the height of each step in centimeters?
s0130: The answer is asked for in centimeters, so first we convert the unit.
s0131: The total height is divided into 24 equal steps.
s0133: Multiplying to check gives the total height.
s0136: The answer 30 comes from dividing the length (720 : 24), and 0.16 from not converting meters to centimeters.

A die used in backgammon (narda) is a cube with 1 to 6 dots on its faces. There is a rule for dice:

The total number of dots on two opposite faces is always 7.

Nodir wants to make a die out of cardboard. He cuts, folds and glues the cardboard. The picture shows four nets (I, II, III, IV) that fold into a cube, with dots drawn on their squares.
s0140: Identifying opposite faces on a net of a cube (spatial visualization)
s0141: Of three squares in a row, the two end ones are opposite each other on the cube. Find the three pairs in each net and check their totals.
s0142: Which nets fold into a cube that follows the rule “opposite faces add up to 7”?
s0150: Rule: the 1st and 3rd squares in a row are opposite
s0151: When the net is folded into a cube, faces with one square between them end up opposite each other.
s0153: In the first net, all three pairs add up to 7.
s0155: In the second, 1 is opposite 4 and 3 is opposite 6, so the rule is broken.
s0157: In the third, only one pair is correct.
s0159: The fourth net follows the rule.
s0160: Answer: B) only I and IV
s0161: So nets I and IV make a correct die.
s0162: It is the other way round: in II and III the opposite faces (for example, 1 and 4, 2 and 4) do not add up to 7.
s0163: In net II, 1 and 4 end up opposite each other, and their total is 5.
s0164: The rule is broken in nets II and III; each pair must be checked separately.
s0165: If two faces are next to each other on the net, they can never be opposite each other on the cube.
s0166: Polls on the New Park Project
s0167:
On March 22, the residents of a city will vote on a project to build a new central park. To find out what percentage of residents support the project, four news outlets each carried out a poll (the outlets are hypothetical):

Outlet 1: 52.5% — poll on March 2, among 500 randomly selected residents who are eligible to vote.
Outlet 2: 57.0% — poll on March 18, among 500 randomly selected residents who are eligible to vote.
Outlet 3: 55.0% — poll on March 18, among 1000 randomly selected residents who are eligible to vote.
Outlet 4: 63.5% — poll on March 18, among 1500 subscribers of a Telegram channel who chose to vote.
s0168: Judging the quality of a sample: randomness, size, timing
s0169: A good poll: the participants are chosen at random, they are actual voters, the sample is large, and the poll is close to the voting day.
s0170: If the vote is on March 22, which outlet's result best predicts the level of support for the project, and why?
s0171: Outlet 4: it had the most participants (1500 people), and its poll was carried out on the latest date.
s0172: Outlet 3: its poll was carried out close to the voting day, and 1000 voters were chosen at random.
s0173: Outlet 1: its poll was carried out the earliest, people had more time to think, and the participants were chosen at random.
s0174: Outlet 2: the participants were chosen at random, and its result equals the average of the four polls (57%).
s0175: Outlet 4: volunteers → the sample is not random
s0176: Channel subscribers and people who choose to take part do not represent the whole population.
s0177: Outlet 1: March 2 — 20 days before the vote
s0178: Opinions can change over a long period.
s0180: Both are good, but outlet 3 has a sample twice as large.
s0182: A large random sample makes the result more accurate.
s0184: Two reasons: the date is close to the vote, and 1000 people were chosen at random.
s0185: Having many participants is not enough: they chose to vote themselves, so the sample may be one-sided.
s0186: The earliest poll is the most out of date; opinions can change in 20 days.
s0187: Being equal to the average is not a sign of quality; the sample of outlet 2 is smaller than that of outlet 3.
s0188: When judging a poll, ask three questions: “who was asked”, “how many people”, and “when”.
s0189: The Best Smartphone of the Year

A technology magazine rates new smartphones and gives the title “Smartphone of the Year” to the one with the highest total score. Six smartphones were rated (the names are hypothetical). The ratings:

Smartphone — Camera (K) — Battery (B) — Screen (E) — Value for money (N)
Alfa — 3 — 3 — 1 — 1
Beta — 2 — 2 — 2 — 2
Gamma — 3 — 2 — 3 — 2
Delta — 1 — 3 — 3 — 3
Omega — 2 — 1 — 3 — 3
Ramz — 2 — 3 — 2 — 3

Meaning of the ratings: 3 points — excellent, 2 points — good, 1 point — satisfactory.
s0191: Substituting values from a table into a formula and calculating
s0192: Find the “Alfa” row in the table and substitute its values for the corresponding letters in the formula.
s0193: The magazine calculates the total score with the formula $\text{Total score} = 3\cdot K + B + E + N$. What is the total score of the “Alfa” smartphone?
s0196: We write down the four ratings in the Alfa row of the table.
s0197: The camera rating is multiplied by three, and the others are added.
s0201: The answer 8 comes from not multiplying the camera rating by 3, and 20 from multiplying all the ratings by 3.
s0202: In a formula, multiplication applies only to the variable next to it: 3·K + B, not (3·K + 3·B).
s0203: Choosing a weighted-sum rule that gives a desired result, and checking it
s0204: In which criteria is Alfa better than the others? Increase the weights of those criteria, then compare the scores of all smartphones for each rule.
s0205: The maker of “Alfa” thought the formula was unfair. Under which of the following rules does “Alfa” score more than all the other smartphones and win?
s0210: Alfa is strong in: K = 3, B = 3; weak in: E, N
s0211: So the camera and battery must have large weights.
s0213: With equal weights, Alfa falls far behind.
s0215: If we increase only the battery weight, Delta and Ramz pull ahead.
s0217: Increasing the weight of value for money hurts Alfa.
s0219: Under this rule, Alfa is ahead of everyone, even if only by one point.
s0221: Only this rule makes Alfa the winner.
s0222: With equal weights, Alfa gets only 8 points, while Gamma, Delta and Ramz get 10 points each.
s0223: The battery weight is large, but the camera weight is small: Delta and Ramz get 22 points each, Alfa gets 20.
s0224: The weight of value for money was increased, and Alfa is lowest in this criterion: Gamma and Ramz get 20, Alfa 16.
s0225: After choosing a rule, always check it against all competitors: beating just one competitor is not enough.
s0227: A seller at Chorsu Bazaar stacks pomegranates on the counter in layers. The picture shows the first three stages: stage 1 has 1 pomegranate, stage 2 has 3, and stage 3 has 6. At each stage, the bottom row has one more pomegranate.
s0228: Finding the rule of a sequence and the next term
s0229: Write down how many more each stage has than the one before: +2, +3, ... What will the next number added be?
s0230: How many pomegranates will there be at stage 4?
s0235: We write down the number of pomegranates at each stage.
s0237: Each time, a row one longer than the previous one is added at the bottom.
s0244: The answer 9 comes from taking the difference as +3 again, and 8 from thinking the numbers double.
s0245: To find the rule, write out the differences between neighboring terms.

As the Aral Sea dried up, a new desert, the Aralkum, appeared on its former seabed. Scientists have observed that salt-tolerant shrubs begin to grow about 5 years after the water retreats from a place. Seen from above, each shrub is roughly circular.

Suppose that the relationship between the diameter of a shrub and the time since the water retreated is given by the following approximate formula:

$d = 12\sqrt{t-5}$, $t \ge 5$,

where $d$ is the diameter of the shrub (in centimeters) and $t$ is the number of years since the water retreated. (The formula has been simplified for teaching purposes.)
s0248: Substituting a value into a formula and evaluating an expression with a square root
s0249: Substitute 21 for t, first work out the expression in parentheses (under the root), then take the square root and multiply by 12.
s0250: Use the formula to find the diameter of a shrub, in centimeters, 21 years after the water retreated.
s0252: We substitute t = 21 into the formula.
s0253: 16 is left under the root, and its square root is 4.
s0256: The diameter of the shrub is about 48 cm.
s0257: Common mistakes: not subtracting 5 (12·√21 ≈ 55), not taking the root (12·16 = 192), or forgetting to multiply by 12 (4).
s0258: Order of operations: expression under the root → root → multiplication.
s0259: The inverse problem: finding an unknown from under a square root
s0260: Substitute d = 60 to form an equation: first divide by 12, then square both sides and add 5.
s0261: Madina measured a shrub with a diameter of 60 cm. How many years ago did the water retreat from this place?
s0263: We substitute the known diameter into the formula.
s0265: To get rid of the root, we square both sides.
s0268: We check the answer by substituting it into the formula.
s0271: The answer 10 comes from forgetting to square (5 + 5), and 25 from not adding 5 at the end.
s0272: In an inverse problem, do the operations in reverse order: divide → square → add.
s0275: Building the longest sequence that meets the conditions, using percentage increase and rounding up to a whole number
s0276: Start at 18 and multiply by 1.25 each time; if the result is not a whole number, round it UP (if you round down, the 25% condition is broken).
s0277: The set must start with an 18 mm coin and contain as many coins as possible. Which set meets all the requirements and has the most coins?
s0278: The next coin must be at least 22.5 mm; to make it a whole number, we take 23 mm.
s0279: Each time, we choose the smallest possible whole-number diameter.
s0280: If we round down to 36, the increase is less than 25%.
s0281: The next coin would be 58.75 mm, which is outside the limit.
s0283: Five coins is the largest possible number.
s0284: 22.5 was rounded down: 22 : 18 ≈ 1.22, so the increase is less than 25%.
s0285: This set meets the requirements, but it has only 4 coins, and a set of 5 is possible.
s0286: 36.25 was rounded down: 36 : 29 ≈ 1.24, which breaks the 25% condition.
s0287: With an “at least” condition, always round up; otherwise the condition is broken.
s0289: A pastry shop sells two kinds of round cake of the same height, made from the same recipe. The small cake has a diameter of 20 cm and costs 120 000 soums. The large cake has a diameter of 30 cm and costs 180 000 soums.
s0290: Comparing the fact that the area of a circle is proportional to the square of its diameter with price
s0291: The price is directly proportional to the diameter, while the amount of cake depends on the area, that is, on the square of the diameter. Compare how much cake you get per soum.
s0292: Which cake is the better buy (more cake for the same money)? Choose the answer with the best reasoning.
s0293: Both are equal, because the diameter is 1.5 times larger and the price is also 1.5 times higher.
s0294: The large cake, because the amount of cake is proportional to the square of the diameter: it has 2.25 times as much, but costs only 1.5 times as much.
s0295: The small cake, because it is cheaper.
s0296: The large cake, because its diameter is 10 cm larger, while it costs only 60 000 soums more.
s0298: The price increased by the same factor as the diameter.
s0300: For the same height, the amount of cake is proportional to the area, and the area is proportional to the square of the diameter.
s0302: For the small cake, you get about 2.62 cm² for every 1000 soums.
s0304: For the large cake, about 3.93 cm².
s0305: Answer: B) the large cake is the better buy
s0306: The amount increased 2.25 times, the price 1.5 times.
s0307: The amount of cake is proportional to the area (the square of the diameter), not to the diameter; the amount increases 2.25 times.
s0308: Being cheaper does not mean being a better buy: what matters is how much cake you get per soum.
s0309: The conclusion is right, but the reasoning is wrong: comparing the difference in diameters with the difference in prices proves nothing.
s0310: If a shape is enlarged k times, its area is enlarged k² times.
s0311: Three Flower Beds in a Park
s0312: A landscape designer drew plans for three flower beds (A, B and C) for a new park. All three drawings are at the same scale. Flower bed B is a circle; the borders of flower beds A and C are wavy and irregular.
s0313: Comparing the areas of shapes by imagining them placed on top of each other
s0314: Imagine placing each shape on top of another: which one completely covers the others?
s0315: Which flower bed has the largest area? Choose the answer with the best reasoning.
s0316: B, because A and C can be placed inside B: their borders have parts that cut inward.
s0317: C, because its border is the longest.
s0318: A, because its border has the most curves.
s0319: All three have the same area, because their widths are almost the same.
s0320: All three shapes are about the same width

s0322: A and C have parts that cut inward
s0323: These inward cuts reduce the area compared with the circle.
s0324: If we place A and C on top of B, they stay inside B.
s0326: So B has the largest area.

s0328: Having more curves does not increase the area; on the contrary, inward cuts reduce it.

s0330: To compare areas, imagining the shapes placed on top of each other is a simple and reliable method.

s0333: Which method is correct for estimating the area of flower bed C?

s0335: Measure the greatest width of shape C and calculate with the formula for the area of a circle.

s0337: Count the number of parts sticking out of shape C and multiply it by the width of the flower bed.
s0339: Measuring area means covering the shape with unit squares.
s0341: Each square on the grid paper represents a known area.
s0343: The errors in the border squares almost cancel each other out.
s0345: The smaller the squares, the more accurate the result.
s0346: A string measures the perimeter (the length of the border), not the area.
s0347: C is not a circle: the circle formula ignores the inward cuts and greatly overestimates the area.
s0348: This product has nothing to do with area; even the unit of measurement comes out wrong.
s0349: Estimating the area of an irregular shape with grid paper is the most universal method.
s0350: Choosing a method to measure the length of a curved line (the perimeter)
s0351: The perimeter is the length of the border. A curved line cannot be straightened, but a string or small straight pieces can help.
s0352: To put a fence around the border of flower bed C, we need to estimate its perimeter. Which method is correct?
s0353: Copy the drawing onto grid paper and count the squares inside the shape.
s0354: Lay a string along the border, following all its curves, then straighten the string, measure its length, and convert using the scale.
s0355: Draw a rectangle around shape C and measure its perimeter.
s0356: Measure the greatest width of shape C and multiply it by 3.14.
s0358: We need the full length of the border.
s0359: We lay the string along the border
s0360: The string follows all the curves.
s0361: We straighten the string and measure it with a ruler
s0362: Then we convert it to the actual length using the scale.
s0364: Dividing the border into small straight pieces and adding them up is a similar method.

The stopping distance of a moving car consists of two parts:
• reaction distance — the distance the car travels from the moment the driver sees a hazard until the brake is pressed;
• braking distance — the distance traveled from the moment the brake is pressed until the car comes to a complete stop.

A table in a driving school manual gives approximate values calculated for good conditions (an alert driver, working brakes and tires, dry asphalt).

Speed — Reaction distance — Total stopping distance — Stopping time
50 km/h — 13.9 m — 27.7 m — 2.98 s
60 km/h — 16.7 m — 36.5 m — 3.38 s
70 km/h — 19.4 m — 46.5 m — 3.78 s
80 km/h — 22.2 m — 57.5 m — 4.17 s
90 km/h — 25 m — 69.6 m — 4.57 s
100 km/h — 27.8 m — 82.9 m — 4.97 s
110 km/h — 30.6 m — 97.2 m — 5.37 s
120 km/h — 33.3 m — 112.7 m — 5.76 s
130 km/h — 36.1 m — 129.3 m — 6.16 s
s0371: Finding a value in a table
s0372: Find the 100 km/h row and read the value in the “Reaction distance” column.
s0373: A car is traveling at 100 km/h. How many meters does it travel during the driver's reaction time?
s0375: We find the row in the table where the speed is 100 km/h.
s0377: The second column gives the reaction distance.
s0379: During the reaction time, the car travels 27.8 m.
s0380: 82.9 is the total stopping distance and 4.97 is the time (in seconds); do not mix up the columns.
s0381: In a table, first find the row, then the column.
s0382: Read the “Total stopping distance” column in the 100 km/h row.
s0383: How many meters in total does a car traveling at 100 km/h travel before it comes to a complete stop?
s0384: Again we look at the 100 km/h row.
s0386: This column is the sum of the reaction and braking distances.
s0388: The car travels 82.9 m in total before it stops.
s0389: 27.8 is only the reaction distance; the question is about the total stopping distance.
s0390: The words “in total” mean the sum of both parts.
s0391: Finding a time value in a table
s0392: The question asks for a time, not a distance: look at the last column.
s0393: How many seconds does it take to bring a car traveling at 100 km/h to a complete stop?
s0394: We find the row we need.
s0396: The last column is given in seconds.
s0398: It takes about 5 seconds to stop completely.
s0399: Values in meters (27.8 or 82.9) are not times; pay attention to the unit.
s0400: The unit of the answer must match the quantity in the question: time is in seconds.

s0402: Total distance = reaction distance + braking distance. The braking distance is not in the table; find it by subtracting.
s0403: At 100 km/h, how many meters does the car travel from the moment the brake is pressed until it stops (the braking distance)?
s0405: From the definition in the text, we know the total distance has two parts.
s0407: We subtract the two values in the table.
s0410: The answer 110.7 comes from adding the values; the braking distance must be smaller than the total distance.
s0411: A quantity that is not in the table can be calculated from other columns using its definition.

s0437: The Amount of Medicine in the Blood
s0438:
At a hospital, a patient was given an injection of an antibiotic. The body gradually breaks down the medicine: one hour after the injection, only 75% of the medicine remains active. This process continues: at the end of each hour, 75% of the active medicine present at the end of the previous hour remains.

Second situation: Bahodir aka takes 150 mg of medicine to control his blood pressure. The graph shows the initial amount of the medicine and the active amount left in his blood after one, two, three and four days (see the graph).
s0441: Calculating a decrease by the same percentage at each step (a geometric sequence)
s0442: Each hour, multiply the amount by 0.75: 8:00 → 9:00 → 10:00 → 11:00, three times.
s0443: The patient was given 400 mg of antibiotic at 8:00. How many mg of active medicine will remain in the blood at 11:00?
s0447: Each hour, we take 75% of the previous amount.
s0451: The same multiplier is applied three times.
s0453: At 11:00, about 168.75 mg of active medicine remains.

s0491: Finding the volume of a rectangular box by counting unit cubes
s0492: Count the cubes in one layer (length × width), then multiply by the number of layers.
s0493: How many cubes does Kamola need to make block B?
s0496: The bottom layer has 4 rows of 2 cubes.
s0499: We multiply by the number of layers.
s0501: Counting only the visible cubes (for example, 12 or 14) leads to a mistake: there are also cubes at the back and inside.
s0503: Finding the volume of a cube using unit cubes
s0504: Find how many cubes there are along each edge of block C, and multiply the three dimensions.
s0505: How many cubes does Kamola need to make the solid block C?
s0508: One layer of the cube has 16 small cubes.
s0514: The answers 48 (only the three visible faces) or 96 (six faces: 6·16) come from counting the squares on the faces, not the cubes.
s0515: The volume of a cube is a³: multiply the edge by itself three times.
s0516: Finding the number of cubes needed for a hollow block (the outer shell)
s0517: For the outside to look the same, all the outer cubes must stay. To find the size of the inside, subtract 2 from each dimension.
s0518: Kamola realized she could save cubes by making a block like C but hollow inside. What is the smallest number of cubes needed for a hollow block that looks like block C from the outside?
s0523: One outer layer stays on each side, leaving a 2×2×2 space inside.
s0527: The answer 63 comes from thinking only one central cube is removed, and 37 from taking the inner space as 3×3×3 = 27 (64 − 27).
s0528: The inner part is 2 smaller in each direction: (a−2)·(b−2)·(c−2).
s0529: Generalizing the count of shell cubes for a hollow rectangular box
s0530: Subtract the volume of the inner space from the volume of the solid block; each dimension of the space is 2 less than the outer dimension.
s0531: Now Kamola wants to make a block that looks from the outside like a solid block 7 cubes long, 6 cubes wide and 5 cubes high, but with as large a space inside as possible. What is the smallest number of cubes she needs?
s0534: First, the number of cubes in the solid block.
s0536: We subtract the two end cubes from each dimension.
s0537: The number of cubes in the shell.
s0540: Taking 6·5·4 = 120 as the space (subtracting 1 from each dimension) or adding up the face areas (2·(42+35+30) = 214) are common mistakes.
s0541: Shell = outer volume − inner volume; the inner dimensions are 2 smaller because one layer is removed from each side.
